# Erythrasma

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Dermatology > Infectious diseases > Bacterial infections > Erythrasma*

[Original Article Link](/library/0k0emT)

---

## Summary

Erythrasma is a <u>skin infection</u> caused by <u>Corynebacterium minutissimum</u>, a part of the <u>normal skin flora</u>. Optimal conditions for bacterial growth are provided by moist <u>skin</u> fold areas. The infection is particularly common in <u>obese</u> individuals with <u>diabetes mellitus</u>. Patients present with well-demarcated <u>erythematous</u> or brown patches with fine <u>scaling</u> and wrinkling in <u>intertriginous areas</u> (e.g., groin, toe webs). The diagnosis is confirmed by coral-red fluorescence under <u>wood lamp examination</u>. Local disease is treated with topical <u>antibiotic therapy</u>, while extensive disease requires systemic <u>antibiotic</u> treatment.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: Corynebacterium minutissimum

* Normal <u>skin</u> <u>commensal</u>

* Gram-positive, aerobic rods

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Moist <u>skin</u> fold areas: <u>Obesity</u>, <u>hyperhidrosis</u>, poor hygiene, and hot, humid climates are contributing factors.

* <u>Immunodeficiency</u>

* <u>Diabetes mellitus</u>

* Advanced age





References:[[1]](/library/w0ahRQ)[[2]](/library/h0Ycfn)[[3]](/library/R0Ylfn)

---

## Clinical features

* Location: <u>intertriginous areas</u> (e.g., toe webs, groin, <u>axilla</u>)

* <u>Skin</u> lesion: well-demarcated <u>erythematous</u> or brown patches with fine <u>scaling</u> and wrinkling

* <u>Pruritus</u> is usually absent or mild.

---

## Diagnosis

* <u>Wood lamp examination</u>: coral-red fluorescence

* <u>Gram stain</u> of <u>skin</u> scrapings: gram-positive rods

## Differential diagnoses

### Intertrigo (<u>intertriginous dermatitis</u>) [[4]](/library/i0YJfn)




* Definition: dermatitis that particularly affects <u>skin</u> folds (submammary, inguinal, interdigital)

* Etiology

* Increased moisture in the <u>skin</u> folds (e.g., aggravated by heat, moisture, feces, urine, <u>vaginal discharge</u>)

* <u>Obesity</u>

* <u>Immunodeficiency</u>

* Friction

* Lack of air circulation

* Secondary infection: <u>Intertrigo</u> is often colonized by fungal, viral, or bacterial pathogens, most commonly <u>Candida albicans</u>.

* Clinical features

* <u>Erythematous</u> <u>papules</u>/<u>plaques</u> → macerations, crusting, <u>erosion</u>, or fissures on an <u>erythematous</u> base

* In addition, if infected with <u>Candida</u>: satellite lesions

* Diagnosis: Secondary infections can be confirmed with microbiological testing.

* Treatment

* Uncomplicated <u>intertrigo</u>

* Topical protective and drying agents (e.g., <u>zinc oxide</u> ointment, <u>petrolatum</u> <u>petroleum jelly</u> , talcum powder, aluminum sulfate)

* Maintaining dry <u>skin</u> and reducing <u>intertriginous</u> friction (e.g., with cotton or linen cloth)

* If secondary infection is present: Treatment depends on the organism.

* <u>Candida</u>: e.g., <u>miconazole</u>, <u>clotrimazole</u>, <u>fluconazole</u>

* Erythrasma: See “Treatment” below.

* Group A <u>Streptococcus</u>: e.g., <u>mupirocin</u>, <u>erythromycin</u>

* Prognosis: excellent in absence of complicating factors (e.g., <u>immunosuppression</u>/<u>immunodeficiency</u>)

---

## Treatment

* General: improved <u>skin</u> hygiene, maintaining dry <u>skin</u> (e.g., with cotton or linen cloth)

* Medical therapy

* Localized disease: topical <u>antibiotic</u> treatment (e.g., <u>clindamycin</u>, <u>erythromycin</u>)

* Extensive disease: systemic <u>antibiotic</u> treatment (e.g., <u>erythromycin</u>)

* Prognosis: Recurrence is common.
